query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The nature of the element X (Si, Mn, or Al) in CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys controls the formation of a coherent, protective oxide scale above 900 °C by modifying element segregation and the resulting oxide‐metal interface structure. In alloys where X is Al or Si, these elements segregate to form a thin, continuous, low‐stress oxide (such as an alumina or silica-rich layer, or a mixed oxide with Cr) that slows oxygen diffusion and repairs minor damage, whereas when X is Mn, rapid oxidation and preferential Mn oxidation lead to formation of a thicker, less coherent scale that is prone to cracking or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state with controlled amounts of X (Al, Si, or Mn).
generation.intervention: Exposure of the alloy to high-temperature (>900 °C) oxidative or corrosive atmospheres under well-controlled oxygen partial pressures.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation tests conducted above 900 °C in environments representative of service (oxidative or corrosive atmospheres), with compositionally matched alloys used for comparison.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, ordered, coherent interfacial oxide scale whose integrity (adhesion, density, and low defect density) is mediated by the segregation behavior of the alloying element X and its ability to form a stable bonding network with Cr (and possibly other alloy components).
generation.mechanism: Element X alters the thermodynamic and kinetic pathways of oxide scale formation. For X = Al or Si, the beneficial segregation at the metal/oxide interface promotes formation of oxides (e.g., α-Al2O3 or silica-rich compounds) that have a small lattice mismatch with the substrate and can develop compressive stresses that heal minor defects, thus ensuring a slow-growing, protective barrier. In contrast, for X = Mn, the tendency to form non-protective, rapidly growing spinel-type oxides that deplete the bulk of Mn results in a poorly adherent, crack-prone oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under prolonged high-temperature exposure (>900 °C), alloys with Al or Si will develop a thin, slow-growing, adherent oxide scale that persists without spallation, while alloys with Mn will show thicker, less coherent oxide layers with evidence of cracking or spallation. The baseline alloy without the additional element X (or with a different X that does not promote interfacial ordering) will not produce as stable an oxide scale.
generation.baseline: A CrFeCoNi alloy without the X element (or with an element that does not favor coherent oxide formation) tested under the same exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys exposed to oxidative or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures exceeding 900 °C; the effects should be observable over realistic time scales (e.g., hundreds of hours) relevant to high-temperature service conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical concentration thresholds and the detailed atomic-scale interactions at the oxide/metal interface remain to be fully determined. Additionally, potential effects of multiphase microstructures on diffusion paths and stress distribution introduce complexities that require further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with systematically varied X content (for X = Al, Si, and Mn) ensuring similar microstructural states. Subject each alloy to isothermal oxidation at >900 °C in a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere for an extended duration. Compare the oxide scale thickness, morphology, adhesion, and chemical composition using in situ high-temperature XRD and post-exposure SEM/TEM along with microchemical mapping.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and growth rate (via cross-sectional microscopy)
Scale morphology and evidence of cracking/spallation (via SEM/TEM)
Phase identification of oxide scales (via in situ XRD or XPS)
Elemental segregation profiles at the oxide/metal interface (via EDS or atom probe tomography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with X = Al or Si do not form significantly more coherent, adherent, slow-growing oxide scales than the Mn-containing or baseline alloys—i.e., if no clear difference in oxide scale stability, adhesion, or growth kinetics is observed among the different X substitutions—the hypothesis is falsified.

Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction

Abstract: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours.
